content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for detecting defects (anomalies) in images. The proposed technique only uses normal images to train a model instead of relying on labeled images of defects. The approach is based on recent diffusion methods rather than GANs, and introduces a technique to improve efficiency by reducing the number of local iterations required for image generation. Also, both local and global image quality scores are used to capture comparisons to normal training images and the global known distribution. Experiments are performed on visual defect detection datasets showing that the proposed method is best in a few cases but not in most.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

Builds nicely upon recent work in image generation using diffusion methods rather than GANs.
Using the two pathways seems effective, and the ablation studies show that using the T-step method improves efficiency.
The evaluations are reasonably extensive within the area of image-based defect detection.

Weaknesses

The clarity of the paper is quite poor, especially in the abstract and introduction. The clarity improves somewhat in sec. 3 onwards. The grammar and language usage are incorrect to the point where it is difficult or impossible to understand what the authors are trying to say. Fig. 1, for example, could be useful or clarifying but it’s difficult to follow. The caption is unclear, especially the last sentence which refers to two noisy images but then seems to refer to one.

This method is for defect detection, where the visual variation in the known classes is relatively small, and defects manifest as localized patches with abnormal visual appearance. This problem statement should be in the introduction, rather than claiming the method applies to visual anomaly detection in general. Visual anomaly detection is not well defined, but is often used to refer to unusual activities in a video scene, previously-unseen objects in an image classification task such as ImageNet, and so on. This method would not work on such problems, where intra-class variation is much higher, and scene backgrounds are complex. I’d suggest calling this problem “visual defect detection.”

That being said, this problem setup does not map onto defect detection problems or applications that I’m aware of, because it is usually easy or straightforward to obtain images with defects in industrial applications that are labeled, at the image level if not the pixel level. The primary benefit of this method, compared with the ones in Table 1 that outperform it, is that it does not require labeled images of defects. But this benefit seems more like a liability since defect images are usually available, and they provide precisely the type of calibration to determine t that this method seeks. 

The experimental results do not indicate any strong contribution from this method. Although the authors point out situations and conditions where the proposed method works best, these are outweighted by the stronger performance of other methods particularly those that leverage labeled anomalies. Even among those that do not, there are minimal or no gains from the proposed approach.

The paper has limited scope, and it’s not clear that it should be included in ICLR. The method is only applied to defect detection, giving a sense that this is really an applications paper despite over-broad claims that the method applies to any high-dimensional anomaly detection problem.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clarity is a major issue in the paper. It is difficult to assess the paper’s novelty because of this, and the lack of comparative detail in the related work section. There are few comparisons to the references at a sufficient level of detail in order to assess the claimed contributions.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is not ready for ICLR, and may not be well aligned with the conference. There are significant benefits to the approach, but the experiments show that the method does not outperform closely related methods significantly.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a method for anomaly detection (AD in images via generative modeling of score-based models. The generative models through stochastic differential equation (SDE) and diffusion processes are employed to capture the distribution of normal data. Two scores during reconstruction are defined to probe the behavior of different types of data: 1) the whole score is the gradient pointing to the high-density regions of the normal data, while 2) the self-score relative to each sample. The whole score of an abnormal data sample is generally large since the defect regions need to be corrected, which can be identified by the difference between the original (abnormal) and reconstructed images (dragged to the normal data density). To facilitate the inference and evaluation, two enhancements are introduced: 1) feature maps in neural networks (implementing the score-based models) are leveraged to capture the semantics, and 2) T temporal scales are adopted to represent the reconstruction process. Empirical results on three benchmarks suggest the viability of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- Interesting method to approach the anomaly detection in images via score-based method

Weakness
- Some elucidation is missing
- Results not quite competitive in some cases
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
On the conceptual side, the motivation that abnormal data reside in low-density regions of normal data has been standard in the area of anomaly detection. The major contribution of the paper is more on the technical part of using diffusion generative models to quantify how far a query sample is away from the normality density. The introduction of the whole-score and self-score seem to capture the difference among the abnormal and normal regions.  

There are, however, several issues to address in the empirical section. 
- The abolition study presents comparison of the proposed method to another one by reconstruction error, which is a common practice in unsupervised anomaly detection. It seems that the latter significantly underperforms the former. Is there any insight into this drastic difference?
- Another critical aspect of AD is efficiency. How does the proposed method compare to other baselines in terms of time cost empirically?
- The proposed method depends on the manually defined T-scales. How to select the optimal T-scales? Any study into the impact of different T-scales? 
- The proposed solution is sensitive to feature maps that are fixedly selected and cannot adapt to different images, which impairs the performance especially on the MNIST dataset. It is claimed that this issue can be easily addressed by some extensions. Why not implement these simple extensions to justify the value further?       
   
The overall presentation is easy to follow, with some typos or grammatical issues (“because goal is to…” => “the goal is to…”) that can be easily fixed via proofreading.

Misc:
- The “AutoEncode (AE)” mentioned in the introduction should be “Variational Auto-encoder (VAE)”. These two are clearly different approaches.
content.summary_of_the_review: An interesting anomaly detection method via diffusion generative processes with some more empirical enhancement and study needed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose an unsupervised anomaly detection method using a score-based generative model. The reason for using an unsupervised learning model instead of a supervised learning one is based on the fact that anomaly samples are very rare in the real world. Based on the assumption that anomaly data exists in low probability density regions of the data distribution, they propose Score-AD as a score-based anomaly detection metric. Two scores are proposed: a self-score that evaluates the distance from the original data, and a whole-score that evaluates the distance from the high probability density region. In addition, a method called “T Scales” is proposed to contribute to highly accurate anomaly detection with a small number of steps.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The authors found that even normal pixels do not perfectly match the original image after reconstruction. Returning to the assumption that defects exist in low probability density regions of the normal data distribution, they propose an evaluation metric based on a whole-score.

2. An efficient method to perform the reverse process in a small number of steps is proposed.

3. The proposed method does not require a pre-trained model for feature extraction, does not depend on other models, and can train models for anomaly detection in unsupervised manner.

4. The authors clarified that direct comparison of the original and reconstructed images for anomaly detection requires careful selection of step t, which is not realistic or reliable. Instead, they focused on the fact that normal and abnormal data behave differently in the probability density dimension.

5. In MVTec AD dataset, the proposed method achieved superior/comparable results to SOTA unsupervised AD methods. Although the proposed method didn't reach the highest score, some issues are clarified for the future work. 

6. The T-scale contributes not only reduction of the computation, but also of the opportunity that normal pixels access other probability density regions.


Concerns:

1. When selecting some feature maps with significant visual effects, what metric is actually used? The authors avoid a normalization process before integrating feature maps, so that the selection process should be done carefully, I suppose. Otherwise, some undesirable regions will be highlighted in some cases. 

2. To get the final Anomaly map, Sw and Se are separately evaluated, and then combined the feature maps at the end. My concern is how to select the {t}, related to my above concern.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Generally, AD is often discussed in terms of reconstruction error such as AE model, in the case of this paper, it is based on self-score. The proposed whole-score model is a reasonable solution which avoids confusion between reconstruction from anormal data and one from normal data. The pseudo codes given in Appendix will be helpful to reproduce the method.
content.summary_of_the_review: The combination of two distance measurement, self-score and whole-score is a new idea, and provides comparable and/or outperformed accuracy in the existing unsupervised AD methods. The proposal of “T-Scales” is also effective way to reduce the computation.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors study the task of anomaly detection in images, presenting a score-based model. The authors present two alternatives to use score-based models for anomaly detection: whole-score and self-score. The method is evaluated on three datasets (MVTec AD, BeanTech AD, MNIST), being compared with some baselines from the literature. In my opinion, the work has some major drawbacks which prevented me from taking a more positive decision.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper addresses an important and timely topic.

Weaknesses:
- There are many English language mistakes throughout the paper, making it hard to follow. Some examples of corrections for the first page are presented next (it would take to much time to correct the whole paper):
> "Visual AD has been critical problems and widely discussed" => "Visual AD is a critical and widely discussed problem";
> "to accelerate inference process" => "to accelerate the inference process";
> "manner while maintain" => "manner, while maintaining";
> "plays key roles in the variety of applications" => "plays key roles in a variety of applications".
- The authors claim state-of-the-art results on MVTec AD, but they did not consider some peer-reviewed methods obtaining better results, e.g. DRAEM+SSPCAB [A]. More such methods are listed in [B].
- The experiments are conducted on small scale and saturated datasets. It is not clear if the proposed method would work on a challenging large scale benchmark.
- Diffusion models are known for they slow generation time. The authors should compare the running time of proposed method with existing methods. Even if the method requires 15 steps, it is still 15x slower than competing methods. Isn't this right?
- It is not clear what is the novelty / contribution of the paper. To me, it seems that the main contribution is to simply apply diffusion models to anomaly detection, which represents a minor contribution.

[A] Ristea et al., "Self-supervised predictive convolutional attentive block for anomaly detection". CVPR, 2022.
[B] https://paperswithcode.com/sota/anomaly-detection-on-mvtec-ad
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper lacks clarity (being full of grammatical errors) and has little novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to the identified weaknesses, I believe the paper should be rejected.

content.title: Unsupervised Visual Anomaly Detection with Score-Based Generative Model
content.abstract: We consider leveraging the deviated outputs and gradient information from generative models due to out of distribution samples in anomaly detection (AD). Visual anomaly detection has been critical problems and widely discussed. However, in many application scenes, abnormal image samples are very rare and difficult to collect. In this paper, we focus on the unsupervised visual anomaly detection and localization task through a score-based generative model applicable to more general cases. Our work is inspired by the fact that injected noises to the original image through forward diffusion process may reveal the image defects in the reverse process (i.e., reconstruction). First, due to the differences of normal pixels between the reconstructed and original images, we propose to use a score-based generative model and associated score values as metric to gauge the defects. Second, to accelerate inference process, a novel $T$ scales approach is developed which reduces the use of redundant information from adjacent moments while leverages the information provided by the score model at different moments. These two practices allows our model to improve the generalization of AD in an unsupervised manner, but maintain a reasonable speed. We evaluate our method on several datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness.
